Requisition REQ-5210: Senior Backend Engineer, Platform Infrastructure

Status: open. Panel: staff engineer (technical round), engineering
manager (hiring manager round).

Must-haves: 4+ years building production backend services; hands-on
experience with a distributed queue such as Kafka at meaningful scale;
comfortable owning a service end to end including its failure modes.

Nice-to-haves: Kubernetes or container orchestration experience; prior
on-call or incident-response ownership; experience mentoring other
engineers.

This requisition explicitly does not require Kubernetes - it is listed
only as a nice-to-have, so its absence should never be treated as a
disqualifying gap on its own.

Tag catalog conventions

Tags fall into two broad categories: skill tags, which describe something
a candidate has actually demonstrated, and requirement tags, which
describe how a candidate maps onto a specific requisition's must-haves
and nice-to-haves.

Always search before creating a new tag. A new tag should only be created
when nothing in the catalog already covers the same skill or requirement
under different wording. When in doubt, prefer reusing an existing tag
over creating a near-duplicate - a fragmented catalog makes cross-req
reporting far less useful for the recruiting team.

Screening verdict conventions

A verdict is always one short sentence: what should happen next, and
roughly why. Good verdicts name the specific strength or gap that drove
the call, not just "looks good" or "not a fit." Reserve stronger language
like "strong match" for candidates who clear every must-have, and use
softer framing like "worth a look" when a must-have is only partially
demonstrated.

Never use a verdict to state or imply the final hiring decision. The
verdict is an input the recruiter and panel use, not a substitute for
their judgment.

Rationale writing guidance

A rationale should be two to four sentences a recruiter could paste
directly into an interview kickoff note. Lead with the strongest piece of
matching evidence, cite it specifically (a project, a scale number, a
technology), then name any gap relative to the requisition's own
must-haves and nice-to-haves - not gaps against some generic ideal
candidate.

Do not speculate about things the resume does not mention. If the resume
is silent on a topic, say it is not mentioned rather than assuming either
way.

Candidate profile: Elena Vosk (excerpt used for prior screenings)

Elena Vosk has applied to two prior requisitions on this ATS, both for
backend-leaning roles on the Platform Infrastructure team. Her profile
already carries a general "backend-engineering" skill tag from an earlier
pass six months ago; that tag is broad enough to stay regardless of the
outcome of any single requisition's screening.

Contact preference on file: email, business hours only, US Eastern time.

Kafka and event-pipeline skill tags already in the catalog

The catalog currently distinguishes between "kafka-operations" (running
and tuning a Kafka cluster itself) and "event-pipeline-design" (designing
the producers, consumers, and schemas that sit on top of a queue,
regardless of which specific broker technology is used underneath).

A candidate who has only consumed events from a queue someone else
operates should get "event-pipeline-design" at most; "kafka-operations"
is reserved for candidates who have actually run the broker cluster
themselves, including partition and retention tuning.

Kubernetes and container orchestration requirement tags

When a requisition lists Kubernetes as a nice-to-have rather than a
must-have, its absence on a resume should be tagged as a requirement gap
with a low severity note, not treated as disqualifying. Reserve stronger
gap language for must-have requirements the candidate does not
demonstrate at all.

Many strong backend candidates have deep queue and service-ownership
experience without ever having touched Kubernetes directly, especially
at companies where a separate platform team owns the orchestration
layer.
